title: Signals, bandwidth and channel capacity
subtitle: Any signal is a sum of sine waves. How many you need is its bandwidth — and bandwidth plus noise sets the speed limit.

sine.title: Sine waves and the frequency domain
sine.body: A periodic signal has a period T and frequency f = 1/T. A sine wave A sin(2πft + φ) is described by amplitude, frequency and phase. The time domain shows amplitude against time; the frequency domain shows how much of each frequency is present.
sine.steps: A signal repeats every 20 ms. Its frequency.

fourier.title: Fourier series
fourier.body: Fourier showed that any periodic signal is a sum of sine waves at multiples (harmonics) of its fundamental frequency. A square wave is sin x + ⅓ sin 3x + ⅕ sin 5x + … (odd harmonics only). Add more harmonics and the edges get sharper — but a ripple at each jump never disappears (the Gibbs phenomenon). The RMS error falls from 0.315 with 3 harmonics to 0.1 with 49.

bw.title: Bandwidth
bw.body: The bandwidth of a signal is the range of frequencies it occupies. A channel passes only a band; sharp-edged signals need many harmonics, so a narrow channel rounds them off. To send a square wave reasonably you need at least the 3rd–5th harmonic: for a 1 kHz square wave, about 5 kHz.
bw.steps: Send a 2 kHz square wave through a channel that passes 0–8 kHz. Which harmonics get through? Odd harmonics up to 8 kHz: 2, 6 kHz (3rd). 10 kHz (5th) is cut off.

nyq.title: Nyquist and Shannon capacity
nyq.body: Nyquist (noiseless): max bit rate = 2B log₂ M for bandwidth B and M signal levels. Shannon (noisy): capacity C = B log₂(1 + SNR), with SNR as a ratio (dB = 10 log₁₀ ratio). Nyquist says more levels give more bits; Shannon says noise puts a ceiling on how many levels you can tell apart, however clever the coding.
nyq.steps: A 3 kHz telephone channel, SNR 30 dB. 30 dB is a ratio of 10³ = 1000. Shannon capacity. Levels needed under Nyquist to reach that (2B log₂M = 6000 log₂M): log₂ M ≈ 4.98 → M ≈ 32.

sample.title: Sampling: the Nyquist rate
sample.body: To digitise an analog signal, sample it at least twice per cycle of its highest frequency (fs ≥ 2 fmax), otherwise higher frequencies masquerade as lower ones — aliasing. A 1 Hz tone sampled at 8 Hz is comfortable (Nyquist ok: yes); a 5 Hz tone at 8 Hz is not (no). Each sample is then quantised to one of 2ⁿ levels: rate = fs·n (here 24 b/s) and SNR ≈ 6.02n + 1.76 dB (19.82 dB for 3 bits).

perf.title: Impairments
perf.body: Three impairments: attenuation (signal weakens with distance, measured in dB), distortion (different frequencies travel at different speeds, smearing the pulses), and noise (thermal, crosstalk, impulse). Decibels add: a 3 dB loss halves the power; 10 dB is a factor 10.
perf.steps: A cable loses 2 dB/km over 15 km. Power ratio = 10^(−30/10) = 0.001: one thousandth arrives, so amplifiers are needed.
